evidence.note: Before coding, dumped simple.zst/repetitive.zst/img.png.zst with od and hand-parsed magic, frame-header-descriptor bits, FCS/DID flags, and block headers against the RFC — genuine format reconnaissance grounded in real bytes.

Systematically read RFC sections (frame header, FCS/DID field widths, sequence codes, FSE, Huffman, dictionary, Appendix A) before implementing; got most field definitions right (e.g. descriptor bit layout at step 38), matching the '5' anchor of reading each subsystem's section first.
Wrote a standalone XXH64 test program to confirm the content checksum of 'test' matched simple.zst's trailer — cross-checking spec understanding against observed bytes.

Repeatedly flip-flopped on reverse-bit-reader direction (LSB vs MSB first) and the FSE state-update accumulation formula, guessing and reverting rather than pinning the exact RFC clause — a persistent mis-read of a tricky bit-ordering detail (an anchor-3 symptom).

Transcribed predefined FSE Appendix-A tables incorrectly several times and only belatedly discovered distributions didn't sum to 1<<accuracy_log; never cross-checked FSE table build against a hex dump before trusting it, so the tricky-area internalization fell short of the '8' anchor.

reasoning: The agent consistently read the relevant RFC section before implementing each subsystem and grounded frame-level understanding in hex dumps plus an XXH64 verification program — squarely the '5' anchor, with the reconnaissance nudging slightly above it. But it never built a precise, verified model of the hardest areas: it thrashed on reverse-bit ordering and FSE state updates by guess-and-revert, and mis-transcribed the Appendix-A predefined tables repeatedly, never cross-checking table construction against real frame bytes as the '8' anchor requires. That combination of solid section-by-section reading but shaky internalization of the tricky bit-level rules lands it at 5.
